pages.text: In 2026, two earthquakes hit Venezuela. Many children lost their homes. Now, they live in tents at sports centers. Five-year-old Elyas lives in a tent in La Guaira. He asks his grandmother why the earth is angry. His home was destroyed on June 24.

He is scared of loud noises like thunder. Many children feel sad and afraid. Experts say these feelings stay in their bodies. Nearly 3.9 million children live in the areas affected by the earthquakes. They need food, homes, and help for their minds. Some children are very restless because they are stressed.

Food is also a big problem. One mother, Claudia, cannot find milk for her baby, Albany. The baby cries because she is hungry. It is hard to get the right food in the camps. Families want to move to new places to find safety.

They hope for a better life soon. The names of the children have been changed to guarantee their protection. This story was produced with the support of Moving Minds Alliance (MMA) through the Reporters for Early Age Children in Crisis (REACH) Advocacy Stories Fund.

Nutritional experts note that communal kitchen supplies often fail to meet the specific needs of young children, exacerbating a crisis that began well before the disaster. pages.text: Australia has a new problem. Bird flu is in the country. It is called H5N1. It is bad for wild birds. Australia was safe from this virus until June 20. Now, many birds are sick. Officials want to help. They are starting a vaccination campaign for little penguins.

Little penguins live in groups on Phillip Island and St Kilda. They cannot fly. They go back to the same home at night. This makes it easy for people to catch them. The birds need two shots. So far, 1,000 penguins have been vaccinated.

Many people are happy about this. But some people on social media are not. They do not like vaccines. Some people use the word "cooker" for them. This is Australian slang for someone who believes in conspiracy theories. It started during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The virus is also in other places. Officials found it in a seal in South Australia. This is the first time it is in a mammal in Australia. They are also checking 28 dead penguins on King Island. Scientists are working hard to protect the animals.

However, little penguins are flightless, live in colonies and return at night to the same burrow, making them easier to capture and vaccinate.
So far, 1,000 penguins have been vaccinated .
A1-A2.headline: Small Penguins Get Bird Flu Vaccines

pages.text: The arrival of H5N1 bird flu in Australia has created significant challenges for local wildlife. Although the virus has affected many parts of the world for years, Australia remained free of it until a case was identified on June 20. Following reports of numerous wild bird deaths, authorities launched a vaccination campaign, prioritizing the little penguin colonies at St Kilda and Phillip Island.

Vaccinating wildlife is challenging because the process requires two doses. However, because little penguins are flightless and return to the same burrows at night, they are easier to manage. While many Victorians support the effort, the announcement triggered negative reactions on social media.

Josh Burns, a member of the House of Representatives, faced significant trolling after posting about the initiative on Instagram and Facebook, with thousands of comments expressing anti-vaccination sentiments. The backlash was expected by some, who noted the presence of "cookers." This Australian slang term, which emerged during the 2021 COVID-19 pandemic, refers to individuals who believe in various conspiracy theories.

Meanwhile, the virus continues to spread. Officials in South Australia reported a mass mortality event involving over 1,000 greater crested terns and confirmed the first case of H5N1 in a mammal—a seal. Additionally, authorities are investigating 28 penguin deaths on King Island to determine if the virus is responsible.

The logistical complexity of vaccinating wild animals is mitigated by the specific behavioral patterns of little penguins. As flightless birds that consistently return to established burrows, they are uniquely accessible for the two-dose regimen required for immunization. In South Australia, officials have documented a significant escalation in H5 bird flu, including mass mortality events involving over 1,000 greater crested terns.

Furthermore, the detection of the virus in a seal marks the first confirmed instance of H5N1 transmission to a mammal in Australia. Concurrently, Tasmanian authorities are conducting diagnostic testing on 28 little penguins found dead on King Island to ascertain if the virus is the cause. While 1,000 penguins have already been vaccinated, the situation remains fluid as officials monitor both domestic and wild animal populations for further signs of infection.

pages.text: In Nampula city, women recently took to the streets to protest against first lady Gueta Chapo. The demonstrators were upset because she failed to provide capulanas, which are traditional colorful dresses, for the upcoming Mozambican Women’s Day on April 7. This situation mirrors political unrest seen after the 2024 general elections, where women wearing these garments were prominent figures during clashes with police.

The capulana holds deep cultural significance in Mozambique, but it has now become a tool for resistance. Protesters used the fabric to shield themselves from tear gas, turning it into a symbol of unity. During the Nampula protests, two people were wounded by bullets. These events highlight a growing trend of female participation in civic life.

As one activist noted, women are no longer just observers; they are active participants in the movement. Human rights organizations have documented the use of excessive force and arbitrary arrests against protesters. Much of the evidence regarding these abuses was shared online, proving that social media is a vital tool for reporting and mobilization.

While the internet remains open, the government approved Decree No. 48/2025 on December 16, 2025, which allows officials to block telecommunications networks. Additionally, a proposed Highway Code aims to penalize those who block roads during demonstrations, raising concerns about the future of public dissent.

title: Caught between silence and visibility: LGBTQ+ experiences in Mozambique

headline: LGBTQ+ Experiences in Mozambique
attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation

pages.text: In Mozambique, there are no laws against LGBTQ+ people. Many people think this means there is no discrimination. However, transgender people and LBQ women face many problems. They face challenges in schools, at work, and in hospitals.

Activists say that silence and invisibility are the main issues. Pepetsa Fumo, a trans activist, says that because nobody writes about them, they feel invisible. In schools, there is little talk about gender or diversity. Officials even removed information about sexual orientation from school books.

This makes it hard for students, and many leave school early. Finding work is also very difficult. Many people cannot find steady jobs. Organizations like Por Ela help women start businesses, but they need more money and support.

Activists say that they want dignity and rights, not just recognition. Digital platforms help activists share their stories. However, they also face online bullying and hate speech. For these communities, real inclusion means having the same rights, jobs, and safety as everyone else.

“As nobody writes about us, we become invisible,” said Pepetsa Fumo, a Trans activist with Transform , an organization working for the recognition and inclusion of trans people in Mozambique .
Economic vulnerability has become one of LGBTQ+ activists’ most persistent worries.
A1-A2.headline: LGBTQ+ People Speak About Life in Mozambique

pages.text: In Mozambique, the absence of laws criminalizing LGBTQ+ identities is frequently interpreted as a sign of tolerance. Yet, for many transgender individuals and LBQ women, the reality is marked by persistent discrimination. This exclusion manifests in schools, workplaces, and healthcare facilities, often operating through institutional neglect and silence rather than overt legal persecution.

Activists highlight that the education system is a primary site of exclusion. School curricula are described as heteronormative, and officials have reportedly removed references to sexual orientation from educational materials. This environment fosters bullying and contributes to high dropout rates among LGBTQ+ students, as teachers often lack the training to support diversity.

Economic instability remains a significant concern. Many trans people and LBQ women struggle to secure formal employment or professional training. While community-led initiatives like Por Ela attempt to foster entrepreneurship, they are hindered by structural barriers such as limited funding. As activist Pepetsa Fumo noted, employment is often precarious, leaving many without long-term security.

Digital spaces serve as vital tools for organizing and advocacy, yet they also expose activists to harassment and surveillance. For the LGBTQ+ community in Mozambique, the struggle is not merely for visibility but for fundamental citizenship, economic opportunity, and democratic inclusion. True progress requires addressing these systemic inequalities across all sectors of society.

pages.text: The sociopolitical landscape for LGBTQ+ individuals in Mozambique is characterized by a complex tension between the absence of criminalizing legislation and the pervasive reality of social exclusion. While the lack of explicit legal persecution is often cited as evidence of tolerance, activists argue that institutional neglect, silence, and systemic invisibility create significant barriers to social participation.

This marginalization is particularly acute for transgender people and LBQ women, whose experiences are frequently erased from public discourse. Educational institutions serve as a critical site of this exclusion. Activists report that school curricula are profoundly heteronormative, and the deliberate removal of references to sexual orientation from official materials exacerbates the vulnerability of LGBTQ+ students.

The lack of teacher training regarding human rights and diversity further contributes to an environment of psychological violence and academic attrition. This systemic failure to provide inclusive learning spaces mirrors broader patterns of inequality that persist into adulthood. Economic precariousness is another defining challenge. Many individuals face systemic difficulties in accessing formal labor markets and professional development.

Although community-led organizations such as Por Ela strive to promote entrepreneurship and leadership among LBQ women, these efforts are constrained by structural limitations, including a reliance on external funding and a lack of management resources. The resulting economic instability is often cyclical, as described by activist Pepetsa Fumo, who highlighted the transient nature of available work.

Furthermore, while digital platforms have become essential for community mobilization and the amplification of marginalized voices, they simultaneously expose activists to sophisticated forms of online harassment and surveillance. As debates regarding digital governance intensify in Mozambique, activists emphasize that the discourse must extend beyond technological security to encompass privacy, freedom of expression, and civic participation. Ultimately, the struggle for LGBTQ+ rights in Mozambique is a broader fight for democratic inclusion, requiring comprehensive access to rights, economic security, and meaningful representation.

pages.text: In Nepal, the Rana Tharu people live in the Terai region. Women in this community have a very important job. They help keep their culture alive. They teach their language to children at home. They use songs and stories to do this.

Rana Tharu women also wear special clothes. These clothes have beautiful colors and patterns. They wear jewelry that tells stories about their history. These things show the community's connection to nature and their past. The women also lead many rituals.

They pray for good crops and healthy animals. They also celebrate festivals like Teej. During Teej, they fast for their brothers and nephews. This is different from other groups in Nepal. Life is changing for the Rana Tharu.
Many people move to cities, and it is hard to keep old traditions. However, the women work hard to protect their language and customs. They are the guardians of their culture for the next generation.

A1-A2.headline: Rana Tharu Women Keep Nepal Traditions Alive

pages.text: In the villages of Kailali and Kanchanpur, Nepal, Rana Tharu women serve as the primary guardians of their community's cultural identity. As migration and urbanization threaten traditional ways of life, these women play a critical role in preserving the Rana Tharu language.

For many children, their first exposure to their native tongue occurs through household conversations, lullabies, and folk tales shared by mothers and grandmothers. Beyond language, these women are central to maintaining artistic and ritual traditions. Their traditional attire, characterized by intricate embroidery, colorful pom-poms, and tassels, serves as a living expression of their history.

Each garment and piece of jewelry carries stories of family lineage and cultural continuity. Furthermore, women oversee essential agricultural rituals and seasonal deity services, ensuring the community remains connected to its spiritual roots. The community’s unique practices, such as the specific way they observe the Teej festival, highlight their distinct cultural framework.

While other groups may fast for their husbands, Rana Tharu women fast for the health and prosperity of their brothers and nephews. Through these everyday actions, women maintain the community’s heritage, acting as the last line of defense against the erosion of their ancestral customs in a rapidly changing world.

Through these everyday actions, women maintain the community’s heritage, acting as the last line of defense against the erosion of their ancestral customs in a rapidly changing world.
